mcqs.question: A fraud-detection text classifier trained on a dataset that is 98% "not fraud" reports 98% accuracy. What should you check before trusting this result?
options: Nothing — 98% accuracy is a strong result regardless of class balance
Whether the model is simply predicting "not fraud" for every input, which would also yield 98% accuracy — check precision/recall/F1 on the fraud class specifically
Whether the tokenizer used subword or word-level tokenization
Whether the model uses a softmax or sigmoid output layer
mcqs.explanation: On a heavily imbalanced dataset, accuracy is a misleading headline metric — a model that always predicts the majority class matches the base rate exactly, here 98%, while catching zero fraud. Precision/recall/F1 on the minority (fraud) class reveals whether the model is actually doing anything useful. Tokenization choice (C) and output layer type (D) don't address the imbalance issue at all.

mcqs.question: Why does NER use per-token BIO tagging instead of a single classification label for the whole sentence?
options: Because sentences can contain zero, one, or multiple entities of varying length, and per-token tagging lets one model handle all these cases by labeling boundaries token-by-token
Because BIO tagging is required only for languages without whitespace-based word boundaries
Because whole-sentence classification is computationally impossible for NER
BIO tagging is an older method that has been fully replaced by whole-sentence classification
mcqs.explanation: A sentence might have no entities, one, or several of different lengths and types, so a single sentence-level label can't represent this — per-token BIO tagging (B-/I-/O) marks exactly where each entity starts and continues, generalizing to any number and length of entities. It isn't language-specific to non-whitespace languages (B), whole-sentence classification is computationally fine, just structurally wrong for this task (C), and BIO tagging remains the standard approach, not a deprecated one (D).

mcqs.question: A translation model produces a fluent, semantically accurate sentence that uses different word choices than the human reference translation. What is the likely effect on its BLEU score, and why?
options: BLEU is unaffected, since it measures semantic similarity via embeddings
BLEU may score it lower, because it measures n-gram overlap with the reference text, and different (even correct) phrasing reduces surface-level n-gram matches
BLEU always scores fluent translations higher regardless of wording
BLEU cannot be computed unless the output is word-for-word identical to the reference
mcqs.explanation: This is BLEU's well-known weakness: it's a surface-level n-gram overlap metric, not a semantic similarity measure, so a correct translation phrased differently than the reference can score lower purely due to reduced n-gram overlap. It doesn't use embeddings (A is false), fluency alone doesn't guarantee a high score (C is false), and BLEU produces a score for any output, not just exact matches (D is false, though a 100% match scores maximum).

mcqs.question: A legal-document QA system must never fabricate an answer that isn't literally supported by the source contract. Which QA approach best matches this constraint by construction, and why?
options: Generative QA, because it can synthesize information from multiple clauses
Extractive QA, because it predicts a start/end span within the actual source text, so every returned answer is guaranteed to be a verbatim substring — it structurally cannot hallucinate new text
Either approach works equally well for this constraint
Generative QA, because larger models are always more accurate
mcqs.explanation: Extractive QA's structural guarantee — its answer is always a literal span from the input — makes it the right fit whenever fabrication risk must be eliminated by construction, even though it can't handle questions requiring reasoning across multiple non-adjacent spans. Generative QA (A, D) is more flexible but can paraphrase or introduce claims the source doesn't actually support, which is precisely the risk being avoided here; the two approaches are not interchangeable for this requirement (C is false).

mcqs.question: An abstractive summarizer produces a fluent summary that includes a statistic not present anywhere in the source article. What does this illustrate about the extractive vs abstractive trade-off?
options: This is expected behavior for extractive summarization, which always paraphrases source content

Abstractive summarization generates new phrasing rather than reusing source sentences verbatim, which gives it fluency and conciseness but also the risk of introducing unsupported claims — the same hallucination risk generative QA faces
This indicates the summarizer is actually using extractive summarization incorrectly
Fabricated statistics are impossible in summarization regardless of method
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the abstractive trade-off: generating new sentences rather than selecting existing ones gives more natural, condensed output, but nothing structurally prevents the model from inventing unsupported details, mirroring generative QA's hallucination risk. Extractive summarization reuses source sentences verbatim and would not introduce fabricated new statistics (A, C describe the opposite method), and fabrication is a real, well-documented risk in abstractive systems (D is false).

mcqs.question: A startup needs to auto-tag 2 million support tickets per day into 15 fixed categories, has 8,000 historically labeled tickets, and needs sub-100ms latency per ticket at low cost. Which approach fits best?
options: Rule-based keyword matching, since it requires no data at all
A fine-tuned transformer classifier, since labeled data is available in reasonable volume, the category set is fixed, and per-request cost/latency must stay low at high volume
LLM-prompted classification, since it always outperforms fine-tuned models regardless of volume or latency needs
Any of the three approaches perform identically at this scale
mcqs.explanation: This scenario matches the fine-tuned-transformer sweet spot exactly: enough labeled data (8,000 examples) to train a reliable classifier, a fixed label set, and hard cost/latency constraints at 2M requests/day that make per-request LLM API calls expensive and slower. Rule-based matching (A) would be brittle across 15 nuanced categories and ignores the labeled data available; LLM-prompting (C) is not universally superior, especially under strict cost/latency constraints at this volume; the three approaches have materially different cost and latency profiles at scale (D is false).
